Comparing panel estimators with cfcompare

Source: vignettes/cfcompare.Rmd
cfcompare.Rmd

The problem

You have a binary-treatment panel and several plausible estimators: classic difference-in-differences (DID), synthetic difference-in-differences (SDID), synthetic control (SC), matrix completion (MC), and the Triply RObust Panel (TROP) estimator of Athey, Imbens, Qu & Viviano (2026). Each lives in its own package with its own data format, its own notion of a “treatment effect” and its own plot. Comparing them on the same dataset means re-shaping data five times and reconciling five different output objects by hand.

cfcompare does that reconciliation for you. You pass one long-format data frame and a vector of method names; you get back one tidy table of ATTs and one plot.

library(cfcompare)

A simulated panel

sim_panel() draws from a low-rank factor model Y_it(0) = alpha_i + beta_t + L_it + eps_it and adds a constant treatment effect to treated cells, so we know the ground truth.

df <- sim_panel(N = 16, T = 9, n_treated = 3, t0 = 7, rank = 2,
                att = 2, noise = 1, seed = 1)
head(df)

The columns are the unit id (id), time (t), observed outcome (y), the 0/1 treatment indicator (w), and the oracle untreated outcome (y0, for evaluation only). The true ATT here is 2.

Comparing estimators 

cmp <- panel_compare(
  df,
  outcome = "y", treatment = "w", unit = "id", time = "t",
  methods = c("DID", "MC", "TROP"),
  se = "jackknife",
  control = trop_control(n_cv_cells = 12L, cv_cycles = 1L)
)
cmp

The att element is a cf_att_tbl: one row per method, all on the same schema (cmp$att). If you omit methods, panel_compare() runs its default set — TROP, DID, SC, MC, SDID, and DIFP (the native engines plus synthetic DID and synthetic control). To run the defaults without a particular method, pass exclude rather than retyping the list, e.g. panel_compare(..., exclude = "DIFP"). The same methods / exclude arguments work in panel_rmse() and rmse_curve().

Every estimate carries the number of treated cells and units, the estimated rank of the low-rank component L (for the native engines), and a note column that records anything that was skipped.

autoplot() on the comparison gives a forest plot of the ATTs with their confidence intervals:

autoplot(cmp)

plot_counterfactual() overlays the observed treated-average path against each estimator’s predicted untreated path, so you can see where the methods disagree, not just by how much:

plot_counterfactual(cmp)

One estimator at a time

trop() is the workhorse. Called on its own it cross-validates the three penalties — time-weight decay, unit-weight decay, and the nuclear-norm penalty on L — by leaving out control cells one at a time and scoring the prediction.

fit <- trop(df, "y", "w", "id", "t", se = "jackknife",
            control = trop_control(n_cv_cells = 12L, cv_cycles = 1L))
fit

The fitted object exposes the per-cell effects, the estimated untreated-outcome matrix, and the selected penalties:

head(fit$tau_cells)
fit$lambda

Calling autoplot() on a single trop fit gives a synthetic-control-style trajectory: the treated-unit average against the estimated Y(0), with a dashed line marking the first treated period (the post-treatment gap between the two lines is the effect, left unshaded so it is not mistaken for a confidence band). Because TROP carries explicit time weights, those weights are drawn as a filled band along the bottom, in the style of synthdid’s time-weight strip. The band shows time weights — how much each period the counterfactual leans on — not observation counts; it is flat when lambda_time = 0 (uniform weighting). Use show_weights = FALSE to drop the band.

This trajectory shows only point estimates — no standard errors — so by default the subtitle reports just the selected penalties (set show_se = TRUE to also note the SE method). To see the fit’s uncertainty, use trop_event_study() (next section). The se = argument on trop() still controls the standard error shown in print(), as_att(), and the comparison forest plot.

autoplot(fit)

Per-period effects (event study)

trop_event_study() breaks the single ATT into per-period effects indexed by event time (periods relative to each unit’s first treated period). It reuses the fit’s resampling — aggregating each resample’s per-cell effects by event time rather than into one mean — so it adds no modelling assumptions beyond those of the fit itself. With pre_periods = TRUE (the default) the pre-treatment gaps come back as placebo / pre-trend points, and autoplot() draws the event-study figure: per-period points with pointwise confidence bars, pre-treatment points shown distinctly, a dotted line at treatment onset, and a solid line at zero. A flat pre-period profile and a clear post-treatment jump are the visual signature of a credible design. The per-period intervals are wider than the overall ATT interval and are pointwise rather than simultaneous.

es <- trop_event_study(fit, se = "bootstrap")   # bootstrap is the default
es
autoplot(es)

Is the effect distinguishable from zero? A placebo test

trop_placebo_test() asks a different question from the standard errors above: could an effect this large appear by chance if the treatment did nothing? It takes a fitted trop object, repeatedly re-assigns the treated units’ timing pattern to randomly chosen control units (where the true effect is zero), re-estimates the ATT at the fit’s selected penalties, and builds the resulting placebo null distribution. The observed ATT is then compared against that null; the share of placebo draws as extreme as the observed effect is the p.value (alternative chooses a one- or two-sided test).

pt <- trop_placebo_test(fit, B = 500)
pt

autoplot() draws the null as a histogram with the observed ATT marked, so it is easy to see whether the real estimate sits in the tail:

autoplot(pt)

This randomization test is the recommended tool for the “is it distinguishable from zero” question; use the bootstrap or jackknife (below) for a standard error and confidence interval on the effect size itself.

Comparing standard-error methods

The point estimate is fixed by cross-validation; only the interval depends on how you resample. compare_se_modes() refits the same estimate under each SE method so you can see how the intervals differ:

se_cmp <- compare_se_modes(
  df, "y", "w", "id", "t",
  se = c("bootstrap", "jackknife"),
  control = trop_control(n_cv_cells = 12L, cv_cycles = 1L)
)
se_cmp

autoplot() shows one interval per method with a common estimate. Zero is always drawn (a dashed reference line) and kept in view, because for inference what matters is whether the interval clears zero:

autoplot(se_cmp)

Recovering special cases

The TROP program nests DID and matrix completion. Fixing the penalties by hand matches them numerically, which is a useful sanity check:

did <- trop(df, "y", "w", "id", "t",
            lambda = list(time = 0, unit = 0, nn = Inf))
mc  <- trop(df, "y", "w", "id", "t",
            lambda = list(time = 0, unit = 0, nn = 5))
c(DID = did$att, MC = mc$att, TROP = fit$att)

With lambda_nn = Inf and uniform weights the low-rank term vanishes and the fit is ordinary two-way fixed effects; with a finite lambda_nn and uniform weights it is matrix completion; letting cross-validation pick the unit and time weights gives the full TROP estimator. Passing an explicit lambda also skips cross-validation entirely — the way to line cfcompare up against another TROP implementation on identical penalties.

Penalty ablation

trop_ablation() runs that whole sweep of constraints for you — full TROP, then dropping the unit weights, the time weights, the regression adjustment, and the combinations that reduce to matrix completion and difference-in-differences. With rmse = TRUE it scores each specification by placebo RMSE relative to full TROP (the robustness exercise behind the paper’s Table 5, TROP = 1.00):

ab <- trop_ablation(df, "y", "w", "id", "t",
                    rmse = TRUE, horizon = 3, n_pseudo = 5, n_runs = 100,
                    control = trop_control(n_cv_cells = 12L, cv_cycles = 1L))
ab

format() renders it as paste-ready LaTeX (booktabs) or Markdown, plot() draws the paper-style table as a figure, and passing se = "jackknife" (or any [trop()] SE method) adds standard-error and confidence-interval columns. Because the result is an ordinary data.frame, it also drops straight into knitr::kable(), gt::gt(), and similar.

cat(format(ab, "latex"), sep = "\n")     # needs \usepackage{booktabs}
writeLines(format(ab, "markdown"))
plot(ab)                                 # paper-style Table-5 figure

Adding covariates

When covariates help explain the untreated outcome, the low-rank term can be split additively as L_js = X_js·phi + R_js (Section 6.2): the covariate-linear part is unpenalised and the nuclear norm applies to the residual R. Pass the column names through covariates; cross-validation is then run on the covariate-residualised model, and the coefficients come back in $phi.

set.seed(1)
dfx <- df
dfx$x1 <- rnorm(nrow(dfx))
dfx$y  <- dfx$y + 1.3 * dfx$x1          # covariate is part of Y(0)
fitx <- trop(dfx, "y", "w", "id", "t", covariates = "x1", se = "none",
             control = trop_control(n_cv_cells = 12L, cv_cycles = 1L))
fitx$phi

Covariates must be fully observed (including treated cells) and flow through the event study, the standard errors, and the plotted counterfactual automatically.

A common counterfactual across methods

counterfactual_matrix() (alias predict_counterfactual()) returns any fit’s estimated Y(0) as an N x T matrix, so methods can be compared on the same grid:

M <- counterfactual_matrix(fit)
dim(M)

For native engines every cell is filled; methods that only define a treated-unit counterfactual fill the treated rows and leave controls NA. This common interface is what lets panel_rmse(metric = "prediction") score the paper’s Table-1 unit-period prediction error across DID, MC, TROP and DIFP (and SDID/SC when synthdid is installed); metric = "placebo" scores placebo RMSE instead.

panel_rmse(df, "y", "w", "id", "t",
           methods = c("DID", "MC", "TROP", "DIFP"),
           metric = "prediction", horizon = 3, n_pseudo = 5, n_runs = 5, seed = 1)

Bringing your own results

If you already ran an estimator elsewhere — say synthdid directly — coerce it onto the shared schema with as_att() and combine it with native fits:

library(synthdid)
sd <- synthdid_estimate(Y, N0, T0)

combined <- as_att(list(
  fit,
  as_att(sd, method = "SDID", outcome = "y")
))
autoplot(combined)

Designs and inference

The native engines (DID, MC, TROP) accept block, staggered, and non-absorbing binary treatments: treatment is simply the 0/1 indicator of active treatment in each cell. SDID and SC are defined for block designs only and are skipped, with a note, on other designs.

By default the native engines report a bootstrap standard error: a unit-level stratified block bootstrap (resampling treated and control units separately, with replacement, keeping each unit’s full time series), the approach used for TROP’s standard errors and confidence intervals in the paper. Percentile intervals are the default; tune the bootstrap with trop_control(n_boot =, boot_ci =). The alternative is jackknife (leave-one-treated-unit-out; it needs at least two treated units), available via se = "jackknife". se = "auto" picks jackknife when there are at least two treated units and falls back to the bootstrap otherwise. These are practical approximations; see Section 6 of the paper for the estimator’s formal inference theory. For “is the effect distinguishable from zero” as a hypothesis, use trop_placebo_test() (above) rather than a standard error.

Performance

The native solver runs on base R by default, but two settings speed it up on larger panels (both via trop_control()):

  • svd — the soft-impute step uses a truncated SVD by default (svd = "truncated"), computing only the leading singular triplets with RSpectra when it is installed (and falling back to the full base-R svd() otherwise). The TROP paper explicitly permits a truncated decomposition for the low-rank step, and it matches the full SVD to numerical tolerance. Pass svd = "full" to force the exact full decomposition; that is what the numerical-agreement checks against the official Python package use (see TROP implementations compared), so the comparison is exact rather than up to truncation tolerance.
  • workers — the bootstrap and jackknife standard errors, the cross-validation cells, and the panel_rmse() placebo runs are run in parallel when workers > 1 (using future.apply / future, if installed). Estimates remain reproducible given seed.
trop(df, "y", "w", "id", "t", se = "bootstrap",
     control = trop_control(svd = "truncated", workers = 4))

Reference

Athey, S., Imbens, G. W., Qu, Z., & Viviano, D. (2026). Triply Robust Panel Estimators. Journal of Applied Econometrics. https://doi.org/10.1002/jae.70061 (working paper: arXiv:2508.21536).
